./src/components/notifications/Toast.mdx
# Toast A short message in a corner of the screen about something that just happened: save...
import { Meta, Canvas, Story, ArgTypes } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import { Anatomy, DocTab, DocTabs, DoDont, SpecTable, States, Status } from '../../../.storybook/blocks'
import * as ToastStories from './Toast.stories'

<Meta of={ToastStories} />

# Toast

<DocTabs>
<DocTab value="overview">

A short message in a corner of the screen about something that just
happened: saved, sent, moved, failed. It closes itself after a few seconds
and never blocks the page.

<Status of={ToastStories} />

<Canvas of={ToastStories.Static} />

Try it: the toast opens in the corner of this window.

<Canvas of={ToastStories.Default} />

## Variants

`variant` colours the icon only; the message stays in the surface's text
colour.

<Canvas of={ToastStories.VariantsStatic} />

| Variant | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | Most toasts: something done, nothing to judge. "File moved to Trash." |
| `info` | A neutral fact about what just happened: "Sync paused while offline." |
| `success` | A result worth confirming because it was not obvious: "Invite sent to 12 people." |
| `warning` | Done, with a catch: "Saved, but 2 rows were skipped." |
| `danger` | Something failed. Interrupts the screen reader. Say what to do next, and keep the way to do it on the page too. |

`promise()` adds a loading toast that becomes `success` or `danger` when
the promise settles.

<Canvas of={ToastStories.PromiseToast} />

<Canvas of={ToastStories.TopCenter} />

## Resources

From npm, or copied into your project through the registry:

```js
import { ToastProvider, useToast } from 'zweihander/toast'
```

```sh
npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/toast.json
```

- Source: [src/components/notifications/Toast.tsx](https://github.com/nguucode/zweihander/blob/main/src/components/notifications/Toast.tsx)
- Spec: [uiguideline.com/components/toast](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/toast)
- Behaviour: [Base UI Toast](https://base-ui.com/react/components/toast)
- Figma: not in the library yet

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="specs">

## Anatomy

<Anatomy parts={ToastStories.anatomyParts}>
  <Story of={ToastStories.Anatomy} />
</Anatomy>

Only the title, or the description alone, is required. The icon box is one
line of body text tall, so it sits on the title's line.

## Measurements

One size. Toasts stack with a gap, the newest nearest the edge they grow
from.

<SpecTable
  caption="Every toast"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Block padding', token: '--space-cluster' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Inline padding', token: '--space-group' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--radius-panel' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Gap, between parts', token: '--space-cluster' },
    { part: 'Title and description', property: 'Font size', token: '--text-body' },
    { part: 'Title and description', property: 'Line height', token: '--leading-body' },
    { part: 'Title and description', property: 'Gap', token: '--space-stack' },
    { part: 'Close button', property: 'Icon size', token: '--icon-md' },
    { part: 'Close button', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--radius-sm' },
    { part: 'Close button', property: 'Minimum hit area on touch screens', token: '--target-coarse' },
    { part: 'Stack', property: 'Gap, between toasts', token: '--space-inline' },
    { part: 'Stack', property: 'Distance from the window edge', token: '--space-4' },
    { part: 'Stack', property: 'Layer', token: '--layer-toast' },
    { part: 'Focus ring', property: 'Width', token: '--focus-width' },
    { part: 'Focus ring', property: 'Offset (inside)', token: '--focus-offset-inset' },
  ]}
/>

At most 24rem wide, and never wider than the window less the edge
distance on both sides.

## Color

The surface takes the opposite appearance to the page: dark toasts on a
light page, light on a dark one. The contrast pulls the eye to a message
that is only there for a few seconds. The tokens below are read in that
opposite appearance.

<SpecTable
  caption="Every variant"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Background', token: '--popover' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Border', token: '--border' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Shadow', token: '--shadow-lg' },
    { part: 'Title', property: 'Colour', token: '--popover-foreground' },
    { part: 'Description', property: 'Colour', token: '--muted-foreground' },
    { part: 'Action', property: 'Colour', token: '--primary-text' },
    { part: 'Close button', property: 'Colour', token: '--muted-foreground' },
    { part: 'Close button, hover', property: 'Background', token: '--accent' },
    { part: 'Close button, hover', property: 'Colour', token: '--accent-foreground' },
    { part: 'Focus ring', property: 'Colour', token: '--ring' },
  ]}
/>

<SpecTable
  caption="Icon, by variant"
  rows={[
    { part: 'info', property: 'Colour', token: '--info-text' },
    { part: 'success', property: 'Colour', token: '--success-text' },
    { part: 'warning', property: 'Colour', token: '--warning-text' },
    { part: 'danger', property: 'Colour', token: '--danger-text' },
  ]}
/>

`default` shows no icon.

## States

<States
  states={[
    { label: 'Enabled' },
    { label: 'Hover', pseudo: 'hover' },
    { label: 'Focus', pseudo: 'focus-visible' },
    { label: 'Pending', content: <Story of={ToastStories.Pending} /> },
  ]}
>
  <Story of={ToastStories.StateExample} />
</States>

- **Hover** fills the close button with `--accent`. Hovering the stack
  also pauses every toast's timer.
- **Focus** is a 2px `--ring` outline inside the action or the close
  button. Focus in the stack pauses the timers too.
- **Pending** is a `promise()` toast: a spinner in place of the icon, and
  no timer until it settles.
- **Entering** fades in and slides `--space-2` from the edge the stack grows
  from; **leaving** fades out. With reduced motion, only the fade.

## API

`ToastProvider` wraps the app once:

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={ToastStories} />
</div>

`useToast()`, anywhere inside it, shows and closes toasts:

```tsx
const toast = useToast()
toast.add({ title: 'File moved to Trash', action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: restore } })
```

{/* Markdown tables do not scroll by themselves on a phone either. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>

| `useToast()` | |
| --- | --- |
| `add(options)` | Shows a toast, returns its id. |
| `update(id, options)` | Changes one in place; only the options given change. |
| `close(id?)` | Closes one, or all. |
| `promise(promise, { loading, success, error })` | A loading toast that becomes success or danger when the promise settles. |

| Option | Values | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title`, `description` | node | |
| `variant` | `default`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger` | `default` |
| `action` | `{ label, onClick }` | One button. |
| `timeout` | number (ms) | The provider's by default. `0` keeps it until dismissed. |
| `priority` | `low`, `high` | `high` by default for `danger`. |
| `onClose` | function | |

</div>

### Differences from the spec

- **Bottom right by default**, where the spec suggests top right.
  `placement` takes any corner or edge centre.

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use a Toast to confirm something the reader just did, when the result is
not already visible: moved, sent, copied, saved in the background. Offer
"Undo" when it can be undone.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={ToastStories.DoUndo} />}
  doCaption="News about something just done, with a way to undo it. Undo is also reachable from the Trash."
  dont={<Story of={ToastStories.DontMustAct} />}
  dontCaption="A problem the reader has to fix goes away in a few seconds. Put it in an Alert on the page."
/>

Keep it to a few words. A toast is read in passing, often half-noticed.

## When not to use

- **For something the reader must act on, or might need to read twice.**
  Use an [Alert](?path=/docs/components-notifications-alert--docs) on the
  page, or a Modal for a decision.
- **For an error in a form.** Use the field's own error, or an
  [Inline Alert](?path=/docs/components-notifications-inlinealert--docs)
  under the form.
- **As the only way to an action.** The toast goes away; the same action
  ("Undo") must be reachable somewhere else.
- **To confirm what is already visible.** A row that appears in a table
  needs no "Row added" toast.

## Accessibility

- The stack is a polite live region: a new toast is announced without
  interrupting. `danger` toasts (and any with `priority: 'high'`) are
  `role="alertdialog"` and announced at once.
- Each toast is a non-modal dialog named by its title, or by its
  description when it has none (as `promise()` toasts do).
- Timers pause while the pointer is over the stack or focus is in it, so
  there is time to reach the action. F6 moves focus to the stack.
- The close button is named `Dismiss`; Enter and Space press it. On touch
  screens its hit area grows to 44×44px, and a toast swipes away toward
  the nearest edge.
- A toast raised from inside a modal shows above it and is not hidden from
  assistive tech by it.

  <Canvas of={ToastStories.FromModal} />

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

'use client'

import type { ComponentProps, ReactNode, Ref } from 'react'
import { Toggle } from '@base-ui/react/toggle'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import { Button, type ButtonProps } from './Button'
import styles from './ToggleButton.module.css'

interface ToggleButtonBaseProps
  extends Omit<ComponentProps<'button'>, 'ref' | 'value' | 'defaultValue' | 'onChange'> {
  // Always a <button> (Button itself may be an <a>, hence its wider type).
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>
  /** Colour of the pressed state. Unpressed is always neutral. */
  variant?: ButtonProps['variant']
  /** Style of the pressed state. */
  appearance?: ButtonProps['appearance']
  size?: ButtonProps['size']
  startIcon?: ReactNode
  endIcon?: ReactNode
  isLoading?: boolean
  isFullWidth?: boolean
  /** Controlled pressed state (the spec's `isSelected`). */
  pressed?: boolean
  defaultPressed?: boolean
  /** Base UI's second argument (event details) is dropped: nothing here needs it. */
  onPressedChange?: (pressed: boolean) => void
  /** Identifies the toggle inside a group. */
  value?: string
}

/** An icon-only toggle has no text to name it, so `aria-label` is required. */
export type ToggleButtonProps =
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly?: false })
  | (ToggleButtonBaseProps & { isIconOnly: true; 'aria-label': string })

export function ToggleButton({
  variant = 'primary',
  appearance = 'contained',
  size,
  startIcon,
  endIcon,
  isLoading,
  isFullWidth,
  isIconOnly,
  pressed,
  defaultPressed,
  onPressedChange,
  disabled,
  className,
  children,
  ...props
}: ToggleButtonProps) {
  return (
    <Toggle
      {...props}
      pressed={pressed}
      defaultPressed={defaultPressed}
      onPressedChange={onPressedChange && ((next) => onPressedChange(next))}
      disabled={disabled}
      render={(toggleProps, state) => {
        const buttonProps = {
          ...toggleProps,
          // Off is the same neutral button whatever the pressed style is, so
          // "on" is always the one that stands out.
          variant: state.pressed ? variant : 'secondary',
          appearance: state.pressed ? appearance : appearance === 'ghost' ? 'ghost' : 'outlined',
          size,
          startIcon,
          endIcon,
          isLoading,
          isFullWidth,
          // Its aria-label reached Toggle with the other props and comes back
          // in toggleProps, which is what Button's icon-only type asks for.
          isIconOnly,
          // A disabled ToggleGroup disables its toggles through state.
          disabled: state.disabled,
          className: cn(state.pressed && appearance !== 'contained' && styles.tinted, className),
          children,
        } as ButtonProps
        return <Button {...buttonProps} />
      }}
    />
  )
}

# Toggle Button A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter ap...
import { Meta, Canvas, Story, ArgTypes } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'

# Toggle Button

<DocTabs>
<DocTab value="overview">

A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter
applied or not. It looks like a [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs).

<Status of={ToggleButtonStories} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Default} />

## Variants

Unpressed is always the same neutral button, so the pressed one is the one
that stands out. `variant` and `appearance` choose how it looks when
pressed. Each pair below: unpressed, then pressed.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Matrix} />

| Appearance when pressed | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `contained` | A toggle that should read as clearly on from across the screen: a filter, Follow. |
| `outlined` | A toggle among other outlined controls. Pressed, it fills neutral and keeps the variant's border. |
| `ghost` | Toolbars and dense rows: Bold, Italic, a star. Usually `isIconOnly`. |

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.IconOnly} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.WithIcon} />

From npm, or copied into your project through the registry:

```js
import { ToggleButton } from 'zweihander/toggle-button'

npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/toggle-button.json
```

## Color

Unpressed is the same in every variant. Pressed and `contained` takes the
variant's solid, as on Button. Pressed `outlined` and `ghost` fill with the
neutral secondary instead of a tint of the variant: a toggle stays pressed
indefinitely, so its label has to pass 4.5:1 on the fill, and red text on a
red tint measures 3.7:1.

## API

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={ToggleButtonStories} />
</div>

Every other `<button>` attribute passes through, including `ref`.

### Differences from the spec

- **Two sizes, not four.** `sm` (24px) and `md` (32px) only, the compact control scale of the Claude apps. The spec's larger steps were dropped; a big call to action is `md` with more room around it, not a taller box.
- **`pressed`, `defaultPressed`, `onPressedChange`** instead of
  `isSelected`: Base UI's names, per the kit's convention for components
  built on it. "Pressed" is also the ARIA word (`aria-pressed`).
- **`disabled`**, not `isDisabled`.
- **`variant` and `appearance` describe the pressed state.** The spec
  applies them to the button without saying what changes when it is
  selected. If unpressed also took them, a contained toggle would look
  pressed whether it was or not.
- **A pressed outlined or ghost toggle is filled neutral, not tinted with
  its variant.** It stays in that state indefinitely, so its label has to
  pass 4.5:1 on the fill.
- **`isIconOnly`**, as on Button.

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use a toggle for a setting that is on or off and applies immediately:
Bold, Follow, a filter. The label names the setting, and stays the same in
both states.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={ToggleButtonStories.DoSameLabel} />}
  doCaption="The label names the setting; pressed says it is on. A screen reader hears “Follow, toggle button, pressed”."
  dont={<Story of={ToggleButtonStories.DontSwitchLabel} />}
  dontCaption="A label that flips to the action reads as “Unfollow, pressed”, which contradicts itself."
/>

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Controlled} />

## When not to use

- **For a choice submitted with a form.** Use a Checkbox or a Switch: a
  toggle applies at once, a form field waits for Submit.
- **For one of many.** Put the toggles in a
  [ToggleGroup](?path=/docs/components-buttons-buttongroup--docs), or use
  radios or Tabs. A lone toggle is independent: pressing one does not
  release another.
- **For an action.** Something that happens once (Save, Send) is a
  [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs).

## Accessibility

- A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader announces
  "Subscribe, toggle button, pressed".
- **Keep the label the same in both states.** `aria-pressed` carries the
  state; a label that switches from "Follow" to "Unfollow" as well reads
  as "Unfollow, pressed", which contradicts itself.
- Enter and Space both toggle it.
- `isIconOnly` needs `aria-label`, as on Button.
- `isLoading` keeps it focusable but inert, as on Button.
- 44×44px touch target at `sm` and `md`, from Button.

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

'use client'

import type { ComponentProps } from 'react'
import { ToggleGroup as BaseToggleGroup } from '@base-ui/react/toggle-group'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './ButtonGroup.module.css'

export type ButtonGroupProps = ComponentProps<'div'>

/** Buttons joined into one bar: related actions that read as a set. */
export function ButtonGroup({ className, ...props }: ButtonGroupProps) {
  return <div role="group" {...props} className={cn(styles.group, className)} />
}

export interface ToggleGroupProps
  extends Omit<ComponentProps<'div'>, 'defaultValue' | 'onChange' | 'dir'> {
  /** Controlled: the `value` of each pressed ToggleButton. */
  value?: string[]
  /** Uncontrolled: the values pressed at first. */
  defaultValue?: string[]
  /** Base UI's second argument (event details) is dropped: nothing here needs it. */
  onValueChange?: (value: string[]) => void
  /** Any number pressed at once. Without it, one at a time: a segmented control. */
  multiple?: boolean
  /** Disables every toggle in the group. */
  disabled?: boolean
}

/** ToggleButtons joined into one bar, sharing one selection. */
export function ToggleGroup({ onValueChange, multiple = false, className, ...props }: ToggleGroupProps) {
  return (
    <BaseToggleGroup
      {...props}
      multiple={multiple}
      onValueChange={(next, details) => {
        // Single choice is a segmented control: once a segment is chosen,
        // pressing it again does not leave none chosen.
        if (!multiple && next.length === 0) return details.cancel()
        onValueChange?.(next)
      }}
      className={cn(styles.group, className)}
    />
  )
}

<DocTabs>

Buttons joined into one bar. `ToggleGroup` joins

## Variants

| Form | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `ToggleGroup`, single | A segmented control: one view, one mode, one period at a time. |
| `ToggleGroup multiple` | Settings that combine: status filters, Bold and Italic. |
| `ButtonGroup` | Related actions that read as a set: previous and next, zoom in and out. |

## Anatomy

<Anatomy parts={ButtonGroupStories.anatomyParts}>
  <Story of={ButtonGroupStories.Anatomy} />
</Anatomy>

The buttons keep their own anatomy; the container only joins them.

## Measurements

The group adds no size of its own. Each button keeps its tier, so a group
of `sm` buttons is `--control-sm` tall. Inner corners are square and each
button after the first overlaps the one before by its 1px border, so two
outlined buttons share one line. The outer corners keep the buttons'
radius.

<SpecTable
  caption="sm"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Button', property: 'Height', token: '--control-sm' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Outer corner radius', token: '--control-sm-radius' },
  ]}
/>

<SpecTable
  caption="md"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Button', property: 'Height', token: '--control-md' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Outer corner radius', token: '--control-md-radius' },
  ]}
/>

## Color

The group paints nothing: unpressed and pressed colours are the Toggle
Button's, and a ButtonGroup's are each Button's. The pressed toggle is
raised over its neighbours so its own border wins where they overlap.

<SpecTable
  caption="Default toggles"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Button, unpressed', property: 'Border', token: '--input' },
    { part: 'Selected', property: 'Background', token: '--primary' },

/>

## States

<States
  states={[
    { label: 'Enabled' },
    { label: 'Hover', pseudo: 'hover' },
    { label: 'Focus', pseudo: 'focus-visible' },
    { label: 'Disabled', content: <Story of={ButtonGroupStories.Disabled} /> },
  ]}
>
  <Story of={ButtonGroupStories.Default} />
</States>

Hover, focus and pressed are each button's own. The focused button is
raised over its neighbours so the ring is never cut.

## API

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={ButtonGroupStories} />
</div>

The table is `ToggleGroup`'s. `ButtonGroup` takes only `<div>` attributes:
`aria-label` names it. Both pass every other `<div>` attribute through.

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use `ToggleGroup` when the toggles answer one question (which view, which
filters) and `ButtonGroup` when a few actions belong together. Give every
button in a group the same variant and appearance, so the pressed one is
the only one that stands out.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={ButtonGroupStories.DoSameLook} />}
  doCaption="One look across the group: only the pressed segment stands out."
  dont={<Story of={ButtonGroupStories.DontMixLooks} />}
  dontCaption="A different variant per button reads as several states at once."
/>

<Canvas of={ButtonGroupStories.Controlled} />

## When not to use

- **To switch between panels of content.** Use Tabs: they own the panel
  and its `tabpanel` role.
- **For a choice submitted with a form.** Use a Radio group or Checkboxes:
  a toggle applies at once, a form field waits for Submit.
- **For unrelated actions.** Lay out separate Buttons with a gap; joining
  them says they belong together.
- **For more than a handful of options.** Use a Select.

## Accessibility

- Both containers have `role="group"`; name them with `aria-label`.
- Each toggle is a native `<button>` with `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader
  announces "Board, toggle button, pressed".
- A `ToggleGroup` is one tab stop. Arrow keys move between its toggles
  and wrap, Home and End jump to the first and last; Space or Enter
  presses.
- Single choice keeps one pressed: pressing the pressed toggle again does
  not release it.
- A `ButtonGroup`'s buttons are each a tab stop, with no `aria-pressed`.
- A disabled `ToggleGroup` disables every toggle in it.
- An icon-only button needs its own `aria-label`, as on Button. A
  [Tooltip](?path=/docs/components-overlays-tooltip--docs) can show that
  label to sighted users: it merges onto the button instead of wrapping
  it, so the buttons still join.

  <Canvas of={ButtonGroupStories.WithTooltips} />

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

'use client'

import { useId, useState, type ReactElement, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { PreviewCard } from '@base-ui/react/preview-card'
import { Tooltip as BaseTooltip } from '@base-ui/react/tooltip'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './Tooltip.module.css'

export interface TooltipProps {
  /** What the tooltip says. Short: a label or a hint, never the only way to learn something essential. */
  content: ReactNode
  /** The trigger: one focusable element, such as a Button. Its props are merged, not wrapped. */
  children: ReactElement
  side?: 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left'
  align?: 'start' | 'center' | 'end'
  /** Milliseconds of hover before it opens. Focus opens it at once. */
  delay?: number
  closeDelay?: number
  open?: boolean
  defaultOpen?: boolean
  onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void
  /** Never open, e.g. while the trigger's label is already visible. */
  disabled?: boolean
  /** Where the tooltip renders instead of `<body>`, e.g. an element in fullscreen. */
  container?: HTMLElement | null
  className?: string
}

export function Tooltip({
  content,
  children,
  side = 'top',
  align = 'center',
  delay = 300,
  closeDelay = 0,
  open: openProp,
  defaultOpen = false,
  onOpenChange,
  disabled = false,
  container,
  className,
}: TooltipProps) {
  const id = useId()
  const [openState, setOpenState] = useState(defaultOpen)
  const open = openProp ?? openState
  return (
    <BaseTooltip.Root
      open={open}
      onOpenChange={(next) => {
        setOpenState(next)
        onOpenChange?.(next)
      }}
      disabled={disabled}
    >
      <BaseTooltip.Trigger
        delay={delay}
        closeDelay={closeDelay}
        render={children}
        // Base UI leaves tooltips out of the accessibility tree; while one is
        // open, point the trigger at it so it is read as a description.
        aria-describedby={open ? id : undefined}
      />
      <BaseTooltip.Portal container={container}>
        <BaseTooltip.Positioner className={styles.positioner} side={side} align={align} sideOffset={6}>
          <BaseTooltip.Popup id={id} role="tooltip" className={cn(styles.popup, className)}>
            {content}
          </BaseTooltip.Popup>
        </BaseTooltip.Positioner>
      </BaseTooltip.Portal>
    </BaseTooltip.Root>
  )
}

/** Tooltips inside share one delay: once one has opened, moving to the next opens it at once. */
export const TooltipGroup = BaseTooltip.Provider

export interface HoverCardProps {
  /** The trigger: a link to what the card previews. Its props are merged, not wrapped. */
  trigger: ReactElement
  /** Usually an Avatar, at the card's start. */
  avatar?: ReactNode
  /** The name of what is previewed: a person, a record, a document. */
  title: ReactNode
  /** One or two lines of meta under the title: role, team, last active. */
  description?: ReactNode
  /** A shortcut, such as a Button. Keyboard focus cannot reach it, so the page the trigger links to must offer it too. */
  action?: ReactNode
  side?: 'top' | 'right' | 'bottom' | 'left'
  align?: 'start' | 'center' | 'end'
  /** Milliseconds of hover or focus before it opens. */
  delay?: number
  /** Milliseconds before it closes once the pointer leaves, so the pointer can cross to the card. */
  closeDelay?: number
  open?: boolean
  defaultOpen?: boolean
  onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void
  /** Where the card renders instead of `<body>`, e.g. an element in fullscreen. */
  container?: HTMLElement | null
  className?: string
}

/** A preview of a person or record on hover or focus of a link to it, on Base UI PreviewCard. */
export function HoverCard({
  trigger,
  avatar,
  title,
  description,
  action,
  side = 'bottom',
  align = 'start',
  delay = 600,
  closeDelay = 300,
  open,
  defaultOpen,
  onOpenChange,
  container,
  className,
}: HoverCardProps) {
  return (
    // Base UI's second argument (event details) is dropped, as in Popover.
    <PreviewCard.Root open={open} defaultOpen={defaultOpen} onOpenChange={onOpenChange && ((next) => onOpenChange(next))}>
      <PreviewCard.Trigger render={trigger} delay={delay} closeDelay={closeDelay} />
      <PreviewCard.Portal container={container}>
        <PreviewCard.Positioner className={styles.cardPositioner} side={side} align={align} sideOffset={6}>
          <PreviewCard.Popup className={cn(styles.card, className)}>
            {avatar && <div className={styles.cardAvatar}>{avatar}</div>}
            <div className={styles.cardTitle}>{title}</div>
            {description && <div className={styles.cardDescription}>{description}</div>}
            {action && <div className={styles.cardAction}>{action}</div>}
          </PreviewCard.Popup>
        </PreviewCard.Positioner>
      </PreviewCard.Portal>
    </PreviewCard.Root>
  )
}

# Tooltip A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the name of a...
import { Meta, Canvas, Story, ArgTypes } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import { Anatomy, DocTab, DocTabs, DoDont, SpecTable, States, Status } from '../../../.storybook/blocks'
import * as TooltipStories from './Tooltip.stories'
import { HoverCard } from './Tooltip'

<Meta of={TooltipStories} />

# Tooltip

<DocTabs>
<DocTab value="overview">

A short label that appears when you hover over or focus a control: the
name of an icon-only button, a keyboard shortcut, a one-line hint. Its
sibling `HoverCard` previews a person or record behind a link.

<Status of={TooltipStories} />

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.LongContent} />

## Variants

| Variant | When to use |
|---|---|
| Tooltip | A label or a one-line hint on a control. |
| Hover card | A preview of a person or record on a link to it: avatar, name, meta and an optional action. |

The tooltip opens on hover after a short delay and on keyboard focus at
once. Wrap a row of tooltips in `TooltipGroup` so that
once one has opened, moving to the next opens it without the delay:

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.Group} />

Only one tooltip is open at a time: opening one closes any other. Hover or
focus the triggers above to see them.

### Hover card

`HoverCard` opens after 600ms of hover or focus on a link and stays open
for 300ms after the pointer leaves, so the pointer can cross to it. It is
drawn like a Popover, a raised surface, not an inverted label:

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.HoverCardPicture} />

Hover the name to open the real one:

<Canvas of={TooltipStories.HoverCardPerson} />

## Resources

From npm, or copied into your project through the registry:

```js
import { HoverCard, Tooltip, TooltipGroup } from 'zweihander/tooltip'
```

```sh
npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/tooltip.json
```

- Source: [src/components/overlays/Tooltip.tsx](https://github.com/nguucode/zweihander/blob/main/src/components/overlays/Tooltip.tsx)
- Spec: [uiguideline.com/components/tooltip](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/tooltip)
- Behaviour: [Base UI Tooltip](https://base-ui.com/react/components/tooltip), [Base UI Preview Card](https://base-ui.com/react/components/preview-card)
- Figma: not in the library yet

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="specs">

## Anatomy

<Anatomy parts={TooltipStories.anatomyParts}>
  <Story of={TooltipStories.Anatomy} />
</Anatomy>

The open tooltips on this tab and the next are pictures: real tooltips
held open and rendered in place with `container`, laid out above the
trigger where they open.

The hover card, open under its link:

<Anatomy parts={TooltipStories.hoverCardParts}>
  <Story of={TooltipStories.HoverCardAnatomy} />
</Anatomy>

## Measurements

<SpecTable
  caption="Container"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Block padding', token: '--space-stack' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Inline padding', token: '--space-inline' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--radius-sm' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Font size', token: '--text-body-sm' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Line height', token: '--leading-body-sm' },
  ]}
/>

The container is as wide as its text, at most 20rem and never wider than
the room beside the trigger; longer text wraps. It opens 6px from the
trigger, on the `--layer-tooltip` layer, above popovers and modals, so a
tooltip on a control inside one still shows. It fades in over
`--duration-fast`.

<SpecTable
  caption="Hover card"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Padding', token: '--space-group' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Corner radius', token: '--radius-panel' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Shadow', token: '--shadow-md' },
    { part: 'Avatar to text', property: 'Gap', token: '--space-cluster' },
    { part: 'Text to action', property: 'Gap', token: '--space-3' },
    { part: 'Name', property: 'Font size', token: '--text-body' },
    { part: 'Meta', property: 'Font size', token: '--text-body-sm' },
  ]}
/>

The hover card is as wide as its content, at most 20rem. It opens 6px
under the link, start-aligned, on the `--layer-overlay` layer with
Popover, below tooltips.

## Color

<SpecTable
  caption="Every tooltip"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Background', token: '--foreground' },
    { part: 'Text', property: 'Colour', token: '--background' },
  ]}
/>

<SpecTable
  caption="Hover card"
  rows={[
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Background', token: '--popover' },
    { part: 'Container', property: 'Border', token: '--border' },
    { part: 'Name', property: 'Colour', token: '--popover-foreground' },
    { part: 'Meta', property: 'Colour', token: '--muted-foreground' },
  ]}
/>

The tooltip is inverted in both modes: a tooltip is not part of the page, and the
dark-on-light (light-on-dark in dark mode) box says so, at the same
contrast as body text.

## States

<States
  states={[
    { label: 'Closed', content: <Story of={TooltipStories.Closed} /> },
    { label: 'Open', content: <Story of={TooltipStories.OpenPicture} /> },
  ]}
/>

- **Closed** until the pointer rests on the trigger for `delay` (300ms), or
  the trigger takes keyboard focus, which opens it at once.
- **Open** until Escape, blur or the pointer leaves, after `closeDelay`.
  Opening fades it in and scales it up from 96%.
- The trigger keeps the states of its own component; the tooltip has none
  of its own.
- The hover card has the same two states, after `delay` (600ms) of hover
  or focus and `closeDelay` (300ms) after the pointer leaves both the link
  and the card.

## API

{/* Storybook's table does not scroll by itself on a phone. */}
<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={TooltipStories} />
</div>

`TooltipGroup` is Base UI's `Tooltip.Provider`: tooltips inside it share
one delay.

### HoverCard

<div style={{ overflowX: 'auto' }}>
  <ArgTypes of={HoverCard} />
</div>

</DocTab>
<DocTab value="guidelines">

## When to use

Use a Tooltip for a label or a hint: the name of an icon-only button, a
keyboard shortcut, one line on what a control does. 300ms before it opens
is quick enough to feel responsive and long enough that tooltips do not
flash as the pointer crosses a toolbar.

<DoDont
  do={<Story of={TooltipStories.DoShortLabel} />}
  doCaption="A short label that repeats the icon-only button's name for sighted users."
  dont={<Story of={TooltipStories.DontEssentialInfo} />}
  dontCaption="Rules the reader needs to fill the field. Touch cannot open a tooltip, and it hides as soon as focus moves on: put the rules under the field."
/>

## When not to use

- **For anything a reader needs to finish a task.** Put it on the page: a
  tooltip cannot be reached by touch, and it disappears the moment you
  look away.
- **For links, buttons or other interactive content.** Hover and touch
  cannot reach the tooltip. Use a
  [Popover](?path=/docs/components-overlays-popover--docs).
- **For a rich preview.** A tooltip holds text only. To preview a person
  or record behind a link, use `HoverCard`. Its action is a shortcut, so
  the linked page must offer the same action.
- **On a disabled button.** It is not focusable, so its tooltip never opens
  by keyboard. Put the reason it is disabled in text next to it.

## Accessibility

- It opens on hover after `delay` and on keyboard focus at once, and
  closes on Escape, blur or pointer leave.

  <Canvas of={TooltipStories.Default} />

- Base UI keeps tooltips out of the accessibility tree. This component
  gives the popup `role="tooltip"` and, while it is open, points the
  trigger's `aria-describedby` at it, so it is read as a description.
- It is a **description, not a name.** An icon-only button still needs its
  own `aria-label`; the tooltip then shows that label to sighted users too.
- The trigger must be focusable: a Button, a link, a field.
- `--background` on `--foreground` reads at 16:1 or more in both modes.

### Hover card

- The trigger is a link to what the card previews. Hover or keyboard focus
  on it opens the card; Escape closes it.

  <Canvas of={TooltipStories.HoverCardFocus} />

- The card is a visual preview, not a dialog: focus stays on the link and
  Tab moves past the card, its action included. Touch has no hover, so
  everything on it must be on the page the link opens.

</DocTab>
</DocTabs>

'use client'

import { createContext, useContext, type ComponentProps, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import styles from './TopBar.module.css'

/**
 * What the shell's pieces need from the App Shell around them: the brand,
 * whether it takes a sidebar-wide cell, where a NavSidebar's top row puts
 * it, and whether the shell is narrower than 64rem, where a NavSidebar is
 * the icon rail. Outside a shell, none of it applies.
 */
export const ShellContext = createContext<{
  brand: ReactNode
  brandCell: boolean
  isNarrow: boolean
  /** The logo for a NavSidebar's top row: the sidebar layout, while the sidebar is expanded. */
  sidebarBrand: ReactNode
}>({
  brand: null,
  brandCell: false,
  isNarrow: false,
  sidebarBrand: null,
})

/** `null`, `false` and `undefined` render nothing. */
const given = (node: ReactNode) => node != null && node !== false

export interface TopBarProps extends ComponentProps<'header'> {
  /** Breadcrumbs, or TopBarNav links. */
  start?: ReactNode
  /** Search, notifications, the account menu. */
  end?: ReactNode
  children?: ReactNode
}

/** The bar above the page. Inside an App Shell it shows the shell's brand. */
export function TopBar({ start, end, children, className, ...props }: TopBarProps) {
  const shell = useContext(ShellContext)
  return (
    <header className={cn(styles.header, className)} data-brand-cell={shell.brandCell || undefined} {...props}>
      {given(shell.brand) && <div className={styles.brand}>{shell.brand}</div>}
      {start && <div className={styles.start}>{start}</div>}
      {children && <div className={styles.center}>{children}</div>}
      {end && <div className={styles.end}>{end}</div>}
    </header>
  )
}

export interface TopBarNavItem {
  label: string
  href: string
}

export interface TopBarNavProps extends Omit<ComponentProps<'nav'>, 'children'> {
  items: TopBarNavItem[]
  /** The href of the page you are on. */
  currentHref?: string
  'aria-label'?: string
}

/** Navigation links across the Top Bar. When they do not fit, they scroll sideways. */
export function TopBarNav({ items, currentHref, className, 'aria-label': ariaLabel = 'Main', ...props }: TopBarNavProps) {
  return (
    <nav aria-label={ariaLabel} className={cn(styles.nav, className)} {...props}>
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.href}>
            <a href={item.href} className={styles.navLink} aria-current={item.href === currentHref ? 'page' : undefined}>
              {item.label}
            </a>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </nav>
  )
}

# Top Bar The bar above the page: `start`, a middle and `end` slots, and `TopBarNav` for n...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TopBarStories from './TopBar.stories'

<Meta of={TopBarStories} />

# Top Bar

The bar above the page: `start`, a middle and `end` slots, and `TopBarNav`
for navigation links across it. One of the three pieces the
[App Shell](?path=/docs/templates-application-ui-app-shell--docs) template places; inside
one it also shows the shell's `brand`. It was `AppHeader` (and
`TopBarNav` was `AppNav`).

```sh
npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/top-bar.json
```

## Search and actions

<Canvas of={TopBarStories.Default} />

## Top navigation

`TopBarNav` takes `items` (`{ label, href }[]`) and `currentHref`. Links
that do not fit scroll sideways, so on a phone they stay in the bar.

<Canvas of={TopBarStories.WithNavigation} />

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `start` | node | – | Breadcrumbs, or TopBarNav links. |
| `children` | node | – | The middle, e.g. a wide search field. |
| `end` | node | – | Search, notifications, the account menu. |

## Layout

- The bar is one row, `--control-md` plus two `--space-cluster` tall, so
  it follows density. Its fill and edge come from the App Shell's top cell
  (solid or transparent), not from the bar.
- In the shell's top-bar layout with a sidebar, the brand takes a cell as
  wide as the sidebar (`--sidebar-width`), so the logo sits where it sits
  in the sidebar layout.
- Breakpoints read the container, which in an app is the shell.

## Accessibility

- The bar is a `header`; inside an App Shell it is the page's banner.
- `TopBarNav` is a `nav` named "Main"; the current page has
  `aria-current="page"` and is shown by more than colour.

'use client'

import { useId, type ComponentProps, type ReactElement, type ReactNode } from 'react'
import { useRender } from '@base-ui/react/use-render'
import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'
import { Badge } from '../../atomic-elements/Badge'
import styles from './VerticalNav.module.css'

export interface VerticalNavItem {
  type?: 'item'
  label: string
  href?: string
  icon?: ReactNode
  /** A count after the label, e.g. the number of members. Joins the link's name: "Members, 12". */
  badge?: number
  /** Replaces the `<a>`, e.g. a router's `<Link to="…" />`. */
  render?: ReactElement
}
/** A named list of items. */
export interface VerticalNavGroup {
  type: 'group'
  label: string
  items: VerticalNavItem[]
}
export type VerticalNavEntry = VerticalNavItem | VerticalNavGroup

export interface VerticalNavProps extends Omit<ComponentProps<'nav'>, 'children'> {
  items: VerticalNavEntry[]
  /** The href of the page the reader is on: that item gets aria-current="page". */
  currentHref?: string
  /** The nav landmark's name, e.g. "Settings". Required: the app's own nav is already a navigation landmark. */
  'aria-label': string
}

function Item({ item, current }: { item: VerticalNavItem; current: boolean }) {
  // The count joins the name with a comma ("Members, 12"), not run on ("Members12").
  const name = item.badge === undefined ? item.label : `${item.label}, ${item.badge}`
  return useRender({
    render: item.render,
    defaultTagName: 'a',
    props: {
      href: item.href,
      className: cn(styles.item, current && styles.current),
      'aria-current': current ? ('page' as const) : undefined,
      'aria-label': name !== item.label ? name : undefined,
      children: (
        <>
          {item.icon && (
            <span className={styles.icon} aria-hidden="true">
              {item.icon}
            </span>
          )}
          <span className={styles.label}>{item.label}</span>
          {item.badge !== undefined && <Badge count={item.badge} size="sm" variant="secondary" />}
        </>
      ),
    },
  })
}

/**
 * Secondary navigation inside a page, e.g. the sections of Settings. The
 * app's own navigation is NavSidebar; this one has no rail, no collapse and
 * no fill of its own, and takes the width its container gives it.
 */
export function VerticalNav({ items, currentHref, className, ...props }: VerticalNavProps) {
  const id = useId()
  const list = (entries: VerticalNavItem[], labelledBy?: string) => (
    <ul className={styles.list} aria-labelledby={labelledBy}>
      {entries.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.href ?? item.label}>
          <Item item={item} current={item.href !== undefined && item.href === currentHref} />
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
  // Runs of ungrouped items become one list; groups stay as they are.
  const sections: (VerticalNavItem[] | VerticalNavGroup)[] = []
  for (const entry of items) {
    const last = sections.at(-1)
    if (entry.type === 'group') sections.push(entry)
    else if (Array.isArray(last)) last.push(entry)
    else sections.push([entry])
  }

  return (
    <nav className={cn(styles.nav, className)} {...props}>
      {sections.map((section, i) =>
        Array.isArray(section) ? (
          <div key={i}>{list(section)}</div>
        ) : (
          // The label names the list rather than being a heading, so it
          // cannot break the page's outline.
          <div key={i} className={styles.group}>
            <div id={`${id}-${i}`} className={styles.groupLabel}>
              {section.label}
            </div>
            {list(section.items, `${id}-${i}`)}
          </div>
        ),
      )}
    </nav>
  )
}

# Vertical Nav Secondary navigation inside a page: the sections of Settings, or the parts ...
import { Meta, Canvas, ArgTypes } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as VerticalNavStories from './VerticalNav.stories'

<Meta of={VerticalNavStories} />

# Vertical Nav

Secondary navigation inside a page: the sections of Settings, or the
parts of a long record, as a column of links beside the content. The
app's own navigation is the [Nav Sidebar](?path=/docs/patterns-application-ui-nav-sidebar--docs);
this one has no rail, no collapse and no fill, and sits on the page.
After Tailwind UI Application UI, Navigation: Vertical navigation.

```sh
npx shadcn@latest add https://ontheshore.biz/zweihander/r/vertical-nav.json
```

## With icons

An icon before each label helps when the reader comes back often and
scans by shape. Use icons on every item or on none. A count after the
label is information (how many members), so it is a secondary
[Badge](?path=/docs/atomic-elements-badge--docs), not the Nav Sidebar's
red one for unread items.

<Canvas of={VerticalNavStories.WithIcons} />

## Grouped

Past seven or so sections, name groups of them. Ungrouped items before
the first group form a list of their own.

<Canvas of={VerticalNavStories.Grouped} />

## Props

<ArgTypes of={VerticalNavStories} />

Every other `<nav>` attribute passes through.

## Layout

- **No width of its own.** It fills the column the page gives it; the
  page decides the column's width and what happens on a narrow screen
  (the Settings template stacks it above the content).
- **Long labels wrap** rather than truncate: a cut-off section name hides
  which section it is. A word with no spaces breaks anywhere.
- Rows are `--control-md` tall at least, as in the Nav Sidebar, and
  `--target-coarse` under a coarse pointer.

<Canvas of={VerticalNavStories.LongLabels} />

## Accessibility

- It is a `nav` landmark and needs an `aria-label` ("Settings"): the
  app's own navigation is already a navigation landmark, so the two need
  different names.
- The current section has `aria-current="page"` as well as the selected
  fill and medium weight, so it is not shown by color alone.
- A group label names its list ("Workspace, list, 4 items") and is not a
  heading, so it cannot break the page's heading outline.
- A count joins the link's name after a comma ("Members, 12").
  Icons are decorative and hidden from assistive tech.
- Tab moves down the links in order; there are no other stops.

import docs from './docs.module.css'

const BREAKPOINTS = [
  { name: 'base', min: '0', px: '0px' },
  { name: 'sm', min: '40rem', px: '640px' },
  { name: 'md', min: '48rem', px: '768px' },
  { name: 'lg', min: '64rem', px: '1024px' },
  { name: 'xl', min: '80rem', px: '1280px' },
  { name: '2xl', min: '96rem', px: '1536px' },
] as const

// One row per breakpoint; each hides itself once the next one is reached, so
// exactly one is visible and it is the active one. Resize the preview to see
// it change.
const ACTIVE = [
  docs.bpBase,
  docs.bpSm,
  docs.bpMd,
  docs.bpLg,
  docs.bpXl,
  docs.bp2xl,
] as const

function ActiveBreakpoint() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.map((bp, i) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={`${ACTIVE[i]} ${docs.bpChip}`}>
          <span style={{ fontFamily: 'var(--font-mono)', fontSize: 'var(--text-body)', fontWeight: 500 }}>
            {bp.name}
          </span>
          <span style={{ fontSize: 'var(--text-body-sm)', opacity: 0.8 }}>
            active from {bp.min} ({bp.px}) up
          </span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function Ladder() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {BREAKPOINTS.filter((b) => b.name !== 'base').map((bp) => (
        <div key={bp.name} className={docs.row} style={{ gap: 'var(--space-3)' }}>
          <span className={docs.caption} style={{ width: '2.5rem', flexShrink: 0 }}>{bp.name}</span>
          <div
            style={{
              height: '1rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-sm)',
              background: 'var(--muted)',
              width: `calc(${bp.min} / 96 * 100%)`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>{bp.px}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Breakpoints Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without modifi...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BreakpointsStories from './Breakpoints.stories'

<Meta of={BreakpointsStories} />

# Breakpoints

Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without
modification. Zweihänder declares no `--breakpoint-*` of its own.

| Prefix | Min width | At a 16px root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `0` | 0px |
| `sm:` | `40rem` | 640px |
| `md:` | `48rem` | 768px |
| `lg:` | `64rem` | 1024px |
| `xl:` | `80rem` | 1280px |
| `2xl:` | `96rem` | 1536px |

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Scale} />

The box below reports the breakpoint currently in effect. Resize the
preview — or use Storybook's viewport toolbar — and it changes.

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Active} />

## They are min-width, and that has a direction

`md:flex` means "flex at 768px **and above**". There is no maximum, so
rules outside a media query are the small-screen case and every
`@media (width >= …)` is an override for larger screens. Write the phone
layout first and widen it; writing the desktop layout first means every
breakpoint has to undo something.

The other direction is expressible — `@media (width < 48rem)` caps a rule
below a breakpoint — but mixing both in one component is where responsive
CSS usually becomes unreadable. Pick min-width and stay there.

## Breakpoints are in rem

`40rem`, not `640px`. A reader who raises their browser's default font
size gets the layout to break earlier, because the layout responds to how
large the text actually is rather than to the device. That is the correct
behaviour and it is worth not overriding: a `px` breakpoint holds a
multi-column layout together long after its text has stopped fitting.

The px column above is only true at the default 16px root.

## The kit has no opinion yet

**No component here uses a breakpoint.** Controls such as Button and Text
Input are inline-sized — they fill whatever their container gives them and have no
layout of their own to rearrange. The stories on this page are the only
responsive code in the repo.

That is expected at this stage: breakpoints are a **layout** concern, and
layout is the [Patterns](?path=/docs/patterns-overview--docs) tier, which
is empty. Marketing sections, dashboards and checkout flows are where
these will actually get used, and where the kit will need an opinion about
which of the five are load-bearing. Most design systems end up leaning on
two or three.

## Container queries are usually the better tool

A breakpoint asks how wide the *viewport* is. A component almost always
wants to know how wide **its own container** is — the same card is narrow
in a sidebar and wide in a main column at one identical viewport width.

Container queries are in every current browser, and they are plain CSS:

```css
.card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.cardBody {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

@container (width >= 28rem) {
  .cardBody {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}
```

When a component is built here that needs to reflow, it should reach for
`@container` first and a viewport breakpoint only when the thing being
arranged really is the page.

## Customization

Breakpoints are theme keys like any other, redefined in the `@theme`
block:

```css
@theme {
  --breakpoint-sm: 30rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Two cautions. These generate utility *variants*, so they cannot be
overridden per-scope by `Theme` the way a color can — a variant is
compiled into a media query at build time, and there is no runtime
variable to swap. And removing a default breakpoint removes its prefix
entirely, so any existing `lg:` becomes a silent no-op rather than an
error.

import type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react-vite'
import docs from './docs.module.css'
import { PALETTE, STEPS } from './palette'

function BandSwatches({ pairs }: { pairs: readonly (readonly [string, string])[] }) {
  return (
    <div className={docs.grid}>
      {pairs.map(([bg, fg]) => (
        <div
          key={bg}
          className={docs.swatchPair}
          style={{ background: `var(--${bg})`, color: `var(--${fg})` }}
        >
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{bg}</span>
          <span className={docs.swatchLabel}>--{fg}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

const LINES = ['border', 'input', 'ring'] as const

function LineSwatches() {
  return (
    <div style={{ display: 'flex', gap: 'var(--space-6)' }}>
      {LINES.map((token) => (
        <div
          key={token}
          style={{ display: 'flex', flexDirection: 'column', alignItems: 'center', gap: 'var(--space-2)' }}
        >
          <div
            style={{
              height: '2.5rem',
              width: '6rem',
              borderRadius: 'var(--radius-md)',
              boxShadow: `inset 0 0 0 2px var(--${token})`,
            }}
          />
          <span className={docs.caption}>--{token}</span>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

function PrimitiveSwatches() {
  return (
    <div className={docs.stack}>
      {Object.entries(PALETTE).map(([hue, values]) => (
        <div key={hue} className={docs.rampRow}>
          <span className={docs.rampName}>{hue}</span>
          <div className={docs.ramp}>
            {values.map((value, i) => (
              <div
                key={STEPS[i]}
                title={`${hue}-${STEPS[i]}`}
                className={docs.rampStep}
                style={{ background: value }}
              />
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  )
}

# Colors Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in `src/tokens.css`, ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorsStories from './Colors.stories'

<Meta of={ColorsStories} />

# Colors

Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in
`src/tokens.css`, with a counterpart under the `.dark` class. There is no
separate dark palette file and no JS theme object — one stylesheet holds
both modes.

**Read them with `var()`** — `background: var(--card)`,
`color: var(--muted-foreground)`, `border-color: var(--border)`. Because
the variable changes rather than the rule, a component written this way
switches theme without a single conditional: there is no light branch and
no dark branch anywhere in the kit's CSS.

**The swatches below read their values out of the live document**, so a
color shown here is the value the components actually get. The token
*names* are still listed by hand in `Colors.stories.tsx`, though — add a
token to `tokens.css` and it will not appear here until it is added there
too.

## Surfaces

`--background` is the page. `--card` and `--popover` are surfaces that sit
a level above it — a card inset in the page, a menu floating over it. In
light mode the page is gray-50, a cool off-white, and card/popover are
white: a panel separates from the page by being lighter, so it needs a
border at most, not a shadow. In dark mode `--background` sits at the
darkest step and card/popover are lifted one step toward the viewer.

Each surface has a `-foreground` partner, and the pair is the contract:
put `--card-foreground` on `--card`, never `--foreground`, even where the
two happen to be equal today.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Surfaces} />

## Subtle surfaces

`--muted` and `--accent` are the same value in both modes and differ only
in intent. `--muted` is for surfaces that recede — a disabled field's
fill, a table's zebra stripe — and is the only one of the two with a
foreground meant for *long-form* secondary text. `--accent` is for
surfaces that are reacting to the user: hover on a menu item, the
selected row in a list.

They are interchangeable in appearance, so nothing breaks visually if you
swap them, and nothing tells you that you did. The distinction is the
whole point: when a brand color eventually replaces one of them, only the
intent that should change will change.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SubtleSurfaces} />

## Solid actions

Filled controls. `--primary` is the default button and **the brand hue** —
blue out of the box, and the one token the
[`accentColor`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves. It
lightens in dark mode rather than darkening, so `--primary-foreground`
inverts with it.

`--destructive` is a hue too, but a fixed one: it stays red whatever the
accent is. A status colour that follows the brand stops being a status —
if the accent is already red, distinguish destructive actions by wording
and placement, not by colour alone.

A note on names: the token called `--accent` is **not** the brand hue. It
is a subtle surface (hover, selected row). The brand hue is `--primary`.
The collision is unfortunate and predates this kit — the names come from
the token contract the registry is compatible with.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SolidActions} />

## Lines and focus

`--border` is a divider or a container edge, `--input` is a form control's
edge, `--ring` is the focus indicator. None of them take a foreground —
they are only ever an outline color, never a fill behind text.

`--border` and `--input` are the same value in both modes and, like
muted/accent, are separated by intent rather than appearance. In dark mode
they stop being opaque neutrals and become white at 10% and 15% alpha
respectively, so an edge reads consistently whether it sits on
`--background` or on a lifted `--card`. That is the one place the palette
uses transparency.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.LinesAndFocus} />

## Dark mode

Every token on this page has a counterpart under `.dark`, switched by a
class rather than a media query, and dark is not a mechanical inversion of
light — surfaces go *up* rather than down, and strong fills get lighter so
their foregrounds flip to dark text. The Light/Dark columns in the
contrast table below cover both.

The mechanism, the three places an inversion would have gone wrong, and
how to follow the OS setting are on their own page:
**[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)**.

## Contrast

Measured, not assumed — every pair below is computed from the OKLCH
values in `tokens.css`. WCAG AA wants 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for UI
component boundaries such as a focus ring.

| Pair | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `background` / `foreground` | 19.28:1 | 19.28:1 |
| `card` / `card-foreground` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `popover` / `popover-foreground` | 20.13:1 | 17.00:1 |
| `primary` / `primary-foreground` | 5.03:1 | 6.79:1 |
| `secondary` / `secondary-foreground` | 16.13:1 | 14.07:1 |
| `accent` / `accent-foreground` | 16.13:1 | 14.07:1 |
| `destructive` / `destructive-foreground` | 4.56:1 | 6.19:1 |
| `muted` / `muted-foreground` | 4.60:1 | 5.64:1 |
| `background` / `muted-foreground` | 4.85:1 | 7.73:1 |
| `background` / `ring` | 6.54:1 | 7.63:1 |

Measured on the defaults: blue accent, gray gray. The `primary` row is the default blue accent. Every one of the seventeen
accents is measured the same way and clears 4.5:1 for its own label — see
[Overview → Accent color](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs).

**`--muted-foreground` on `--muted` is 4.60:1 in light mode**, the
tightest pair it forms. It used to be 4.34:1, under AA: gray-500 on every
ramp has since been darkened to the lightest value that clears 4.6:1 on
its own gray-100, so muted text can now sit on a muted fill. On the page background, where secondary
text usually lives, the same token is 4.85:1.

**`--subtle-foreground` is a step between body text and muted text**
(gray-600 light, gray-300 dark): navigation labels that should recede
until hovered or current, as in the Claude apps' sidebar. It reads about
7.5:1 on the light page, so it is body-safe; use `--muted-foreground` for
genuinely secondary text.

**`--surface-filled` is a filled panel that muted text can sit on.**
Muted text reads 4.85:1 on it (gray-50) and 5.64:1 on gray-800 in dark — a step off `--card` so a filled panel still reads as filled. The build
measures `--muted-foreground` on `--background`, `--card`,
`--surface-filled` and `--muted` in both modes on all nine gray ramps, and
stops if any pair drops under 4.5:1. The tightest is neutral on `--muted`,
at 4.60:1.

**`--control-border` outlines a checkbox, radio or switch track.** Those
controls have nothing else that shows they are there, so WCAG 1.4.11 wants
3:1 against the page — and `--input` (gray-200) is about 1.3:1. The build
measures it on all nine gray ramps.

**`--field-border` is the text-field edge** (gray-300 light, white 18%
dark), about 1.5:1: the light hairline of the Claude apps, and a
deliberate exception to 3:1 for fields only. Fields lean on a white
`--card` fill, a faint drop, the label and the focus ring instead. A
product that needs 3:1 sets `--field-border: var(--control-border)`.

**`--primary-text` is the brand hue as text** — an outlined or ghost
primary button. The solid is picked for its label, not for being read on
the page, and amber-500 on white is barely 2:1, so the build measures a
third step per accent that clears 4.5:1 against the page.

**Two values are deliberately off the beaten path.** `--ring` follows the
accent at its `-700` step rather than being a neutral, because a focus
indicator has to clear 3:1 against the page under WCAG 1.4.11 and the
lighter solids miss it — yellow-600 measures 2.93:1, so the ring uses a
step darker than the fill for every accent.
And dark `--destructive-foreground` is neutral-900 rather than near-white:
dark mode inverts the destructive fill to red-400, and near-white on
red-400 is 2.77:1, which makes the label of a destructive button in dark
mode fail AA outright.

## Status

Four fixed hues for messages about state: `info` (blue), `success`
(green), `warning` (amber), `danger` (red). Like `--destructive`, they do
not follow the accent. Each comes as four tokens:

| Token | Use | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--{status}` | Solid fill | 600 (green 700, amber 500) | 400 |
| `--{status}-foreground` | Label on the solid | neutral-50 (amber: neutral-900) | neutral-900 |
| `--{status}-subtle` | Tinted fill | 100 | 950 |
| `--{status}-text` | Text, icon and border on the tint or the page | 800 | 300 |

The steps are pinned by hand, so `npm run tokens` measures them and fails
the build if any pair drops under 4.5:1:

| Pair | info | success | warning | danger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| label on solid, light | 5.03:1 | 4.73:1 | 8.35:1 | 4.56:1 |
| text on subtle, light | 7.25:1 | 6.45:1 | 6.41:1 | 6.86:1 |
| text on page, light | 8.84:1 | 7.09:1 | 7.13:1 | 8.37:1 |
| label on solid, dark | 6.79:1 | 10.09:1 | 10.43:1 | 6.19:1 |
| text on subtle, dark | 8.13:1 | 10.67:1 | 10.37:1 | 8.40:1 |
| text on page, dark | 10.93:1 | 14.16:1 | 13.69:1 | 10.30:1 |

`danger` and `destructive` share red-600 but mean different things:
`destructive` is an action that destroys, `danger` is a state that is
wrong. Keep them apart so either can move without the other.

## Color is never the only signal

`--destructive` on a button does not say what will be destroyed, and a red
badge means nothing to a reader who cannot distinguish it from a neutral
one. Pair color with words, an icon, or a shape every time it carries
meaning. The contrast numbers above are a floor, not a design review.

## Where the values come from

**Every value is a step off a published ramp, digit for digit.** Nothing
here was hand-picked or eyeballed. Two ramps feed the palette and each is
swappable on its own: an **accent** (blue by default) for `--primary` and
`--ring`, and a **gray** (the `gray` ramp by default) for everything structural.

| Token | Light | Dark | Driven by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `background` | gray-50 | gray-950 | gray |
| `foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `card`, `popover` | white | gray-900 | gray |
| `card-foreground`, `popover-foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `primary` | accent-600 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-foreground` | white or near-black | near-black | **accent** |
| `secondary`, `muted`, `accent` | gray-100 | gray-800 | gray |
| `secondary-foreground`, `accent-foreground` | gray-900 | gray-50 | gray |
| `selected` | gray-200 | white 10% | gray |
| `hover-overlay` | black 5% | white 6% | fixed |
| `scrim` | black 50% | black 50% | fixed |
| `muted-foreground` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `subtle-foreground` | gray-600 | gray-300 | gray |
| `surface-filled` | gray-50 | gray-800 | gray |
| `neutral-solid` | gray-600 | gray-600 | gray |
| `neutral-solid-foreground` | gray-50 | gray-50 | gray |
| `destructive` | red-600 | red-400 | fixed |
| `destructive-foreground` | neutral-50 | neutral-900 | fixed |
| `border`, `input` | gray-200 | white 10% / 15% | gray |
| `field-border` | gray-300 | white 18% | gray |
| `control-border` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `ring` | accent-700 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-text` | first of accent-600…900 at 4.5:1 on the light page | first of accent-400…200 at 4.5:1 on the dark page | **accent** |

The light accent step is `-600` for most hues but `-700` for sky, fuchsia,
pink and rose, and the label is white or near-black depending on which one
clears 4.5:1 on that fill — the warm hues take dark labels. Exceptions to
the ramp rule: light `--card`/`--popover` (pure white, so a panel reads
lighter than the gray-50 page) and dark `--border`/`--input`/`--selected`, and `--hover-overlay` in both
(alpha, so they work over any surface — the sidebar's hover sits on
`--surface-filled`, which in dark equals the opaque `--accent` fill).

`--destructive` deliberately does **not** follow the accent. A status
colour that changes with the brand stops being a status.

## Naming

Token names describe a **role**, not a property or a color. `--primary` is
not "the brand color" and `--destructive` is not "red"; they are the
default action and the dangerous one. The names are also the common
contract most token-based kits share, which is what lets a component
copied out of Zweihänder resolve against tokens a target project already
has instead of arriving with its own private palette.

Figma, by contrast, conventionally names tokens by property —
`bg/primary`, `text/primary`, `border/default`. Those do not map one to
one: Figma's `text/primary` is this system's `--foreground`, and its
`bg/primary` is `--background`. Neither is `--primary`. Worth pinning down
before any Figma sync, since the collision is silent.

## Primitives

The full underlying palette — 22 hues × 11 shades. None of these
classes are referenced anywhere in the kit, so they are force-generated by
an `@source inline(...)` directive in `src/index.css` purely so this page
can render them.

This is raw material, not a palette to build UI from. Reach for a
primitive when you are defining the *next* semantic token; if a primitive
shows up in a component, a token is missing.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Primitives} />

## Customization

Swap the raw values in `:root` and `.dark` in `src/tokens.css`. Nothing
that reads `var(--primary)` or `var(--muted-foreground)` changes, because
every rule points at the variable rather than the value.

Two things to carry through a rebrand: re-measure the pairs in the
contrast table — a brand hue at the same *lightness* as neutral-900 will
not necessarily hit the same ratios — and keep light and dark as separate
decisions. Lifting a brand color for dark mode by reusing the light value
is what produces the 2.77:1 failure documented above.

Projects that install through the registry get these values merged into
their own stylesheet; projects on the npm package import
`zweihander/tokens.css` and override afterwards.

# Cursors Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do not get ...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CursorsStories from './Cursors.stories'

<Meta of={CursorsStories} />

# Cursors

Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do
not get `cursor: pointer`. Links do.**

## The convention

`cursor: pointer` means "this navigates" — it is the hand that appears
over a link. Browsers have never applied it to `<button>`, `<select>` or a
checkbox, and neither does this kit. Interactive elements that act on the
current page keep the regular arrow; only a link gets the hand. This is a
deliberate departure from the very common `button { cursor: pointer }`
reset.

It is worth knowing the argument on the other side: a large body of
usability opinion holds that the hand cursor is now such a widespread
affordance for "clickable" that removing it costs more than the semantic
purity gains. If your product takes that view, this is a one-line change —
see **Customization** below. The point of making it a token is that it is
one line, in one place, rather than a decision re-litigated per component.

<Canvas of={CursorsStories.Tokens} />

## `--cursor-button`

`default` — the regular arrow. Applied by Button.

Note this changes nothing visually today: a native `<button>` already
shows the arrow. **The token's job is not its current value; it is that
the value is reachable.** Without it, switching the kit to `pointer` means
editing every component; with it, it is one declaration.

## `--cursor-link`

`pointer` — the hand.

This one exists because the convention above has a second half that is
easy to state and easy to get wrong. Button takes `href`, so it can
render as a real `<a href>` — and when it did, it inherited
`--cursor-button` and lost the hand that the browser gives every other
link on the page. A link styled as a button is still a link.

```css
a[href].button {
  cursor: var(--cursor-link);
}
```

The `a[href]` part is doing real work. An `<a>` without `href` is not a
link and browsers do not give it the hand either, so matching on the
attribute rather than the element keeps the rule honest.

The distinction the kit draws is navigation versus action, not
appearance: a `<button>` styled as a link would still act on the current
page, so it would keep the arrow.

| | Element | Cursor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<Button>` | `<button>` | arrow |
| `<Button href="/x">` | `<a href>` | hand |

The Button `Href` story asserts this, and compares against a bare
`<a href>` rather than the literal `pointer` — so overriding
`--cursor-link` moves the assertion with it instead of breaking it.

## `--cursor-disabled`

`not-allowed` — used by TextInput, and **not** by Button. That asymmetry
is not an oversight.

A disabled `<input>` stays hit-testable, so a cursor set on it renders and
the user gets feedback on hover. Button's disabled state is
`pointer-events: none`, which makes the element untargetable; an
untargetable element is never hovered, so a cursor there would be dead
CSS. The `pointer-events: none` is not incidental — because Button
can render as an `<a>`, which ignores the `disabled` attribute entirely. Blocking pointer events is what actually disables it
in that case.

So the token applies to the pattern where a control stays hoverable while
disabled — including a control deliberately wrapped so a tooltip can
explain *why*. That trade-off, between a disabled control you can
interrogate and one that is inert, is a real design choice, and the two
components here happen to sit on opposite sides of it.

## Adding tokens

A mature system ends up with a token per interactive component —
checkboxes, menu items, radios, switches, slider thumbs. This kit has
three, because it has two components and one of them can render as two
different things.

{/* docs:check allow --cursor-slider-thumb -- an example of a token not to add */}

**Add a token when the component that needs it is built, not before.** A
`--cursor-slider-thumb` with no Slider is a value nobody can verify and
that the eventual Slider may not want.

## Customization

All three are plain CSS keywords, not colors, so they override like any
other custom property:

```css
:root {
  --cursor-button: pointer;
}
```

Load any override after Zweihänder's own stylesheet so the cascade picks it
up. Setting `--cursor-button: pointer` is the one-line version of adopting
the mainstream convention; it leaves `--cursor-link` alone, which is
already `pointer`, so the two simply converge.

# Dark mode Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the light v...
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DarkModeStories from './DarkMode.stories'

<Meta of={DarkModeStories} />

# Dark mode

Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the
light values on `:root, .light` and the dark values on `.dark`, and
Every rule in the kit reads those variables, so the class is the only
switch there is. The same scopes set `color-scheme`, so the UI the browser
draws itself (scrollbars, date and select popups, autofill) switches with
them.

Nothing is automatic about it. Adding `class="dark"` to `<html>` is what
switches the document; without that, a device set to dark mode gets the
light theme. That is the trade — see **Following the system** below.

<Canvas of={DarkModeStories.SideBySide} />

## Components don't know about it

No component stylesheet — `Button.module.css`, `InputField.module.css` or any other — mentions `.dark`.
They write `background: var(--primary)`, and it is the variable that
changes; the rule is identical in both modes.

This is the main reason to reach for a token rather than a literal. A
hard-coded `#0a0a0a` is near-black in both modes and needs a `.dark`
override beside it to survive a theme switch; `var(--primary)` needs
nothing. Every theme conditional in a codebase is a place a value was
hardcoded and then patched.

## Dark is not an inversion

Flipping lightness would produce the wrong result in three places, and the
palette deliberately doesn't:

- **`--background` is neutral-950, not black.** A pure-black page makes
  the halation around light text worse and leaves no room to sit a surface
  *below* the page level.
- **Surfaces go up, not down.** `--card` and `--popover` are a step
  *lighter* than the page in dark mode and identical to it in light mode.
  Elevation in dark mode is carried by lightness, because a drop shadow
  has almost nothing left to darken (see
  [Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)).
- **Strong fills become light, so their labels become dark.**
  `--primary` goes from near-black to near-white, and
  `--primary-foreground` inverts with it. `--destructive` does the same,
  red-600 to red-400 — which is exactly where the palette's one contrast
  bug lived: keeping the near-white label on the lightened red measured
  2.77:1. It is now neutral-900 at 6.19:1. Inverting a fill without
  inverting its foreground is the single easiest dark-mode mistake to
  make.

Full measurements for both modes are in
[Color → Contrast](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs).

## Alpha for edges

`--border` and `--input` are the one place the palette uses transparency:
opaque neutral-200 in light, `white / 10%` and `white / 15%` in dark. An
opaque dark border would have to be re-chosen for every surface it sits
on; a translucent white edge lightens whatever is underneath, so the same
token reads correctly on `--background` and on a lifted `--card`.

## Scoping

`Theme` switches an appearance for a subtree rather than the document —
a dark footer on a light page, a light popover inside a dark shell. See
[Overview → Nesting](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) for how the
nesting resolves and the one caveat that comes with it.

```tsx
<Theme appearance="dark">
  <Footer />
</Theme>
```

## Following the system

The kit ships no `prefers-color-scheme` handling, because the choice
between "follow the OS" and "remember what the user picked" belongs to the
app, not the component library. The usual shape:

```ts
const media = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')
const stored = localStorage.getItem('theme') // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const dark = stored ? stored === 'dark' : media.matches
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark)
```

Two things worth getting right. Run it **before first paint** — in a
blocking inline script in `<head>`, not in a `useEffect` — or the page
renders light and flips, which is the flash every themed site has had at
some point. And keep listening to `media` afterwards so a user changing
their OS setting mid-session is followed, unless they have made an
explicit choice.

In this Storybook, the **Theme** toolbar control does the class toggle for
you; there is no persistence and no system detection.

export const Tabs: Story = {
  render: () => tabs,
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    await expect(canvas.getByRole('tablist', { name: 'Documentation' })).toBeVisible()
    const [overview, specs, guidelines] = canvas.getAllByRole('tab')
    await expect([overview, specs, guidelines].map((t) => t.textContent)).toEqual(['Overview', 'Specs', 'Guidelines'])

    await expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('What it is.')
    // Mouse.
    await userEvent.click(specs)
    await waitFor(() => expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('How it is built.'))
    // Arrow keys select as they move: a docs page, not a toolbar.
    await userEvent.keyboard('{ArrowRight}')
    await waitFor(() => expect(guidelines).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true'))
    await waitFor(() => expect(canvas.getByRole('tabpanel')).toHaveTextContent('How to use it.'))
    await userEvent.keyboard('{ArrowLeft}{ArrowLeft}')
    await waitFor(() => expect(overview).toHaveAttribute('aria-selected', 'true'))
    await expect(overview).toHaveFocus()
  },
}

export const AnatomyMarkers: Story = {
  name: 'Anatomy',
  render: () => anatomy,
  play: async ({ canvas }) => {
    // One marker per part, each named by number and part.
    const markers = await canvas.findAllByRole('img', { name: /^\d: / })
    await expect(markers.map((m) => m.getAttribute('aria-label'))).toEqual(['1: Container', '2: Start icon'])
    await expect(markers.map((m) => m.textContent)).toEqual(['1', '2'])
    // Each sits above its part, centred on it, with a line down to the part.
    for (const [marker, part] of [
      [markers[0], canvas.getByRole('button')],
      [markers[1], canvas.getByRole('button').querySelector('svg')!],
    ] as const) {
      const m = marker.getBoundingClientRect()
      const p = part.getBoundingClientRect()
      await expect(Math.abs(m.left + m.width / 2 - (p.left + p.width / 2))).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)
      await expect(m.bottom).toBeLessThan(p.top)
      const line = (marker.previousElementSibling as HTMLElement).getBoundingClientRect()
      await expect(Math.abs(line.bottom - p.top)).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1)
    }
    // The key lists every part.
    const key = canvas.getByRole('table')
    await expect(within(key).getByRole('rowheader', { name: 'Start icon' })).toBeVisible()
    await expect(key).not.toHaveTextContent('Not found')
    // Backticks in a description become inline code.
    await expect(within(key).getByText('aria-hidden').tagName).toBe('CODE')
    await expect(key).not.toHaveTextContent('`')
  },
}

    await expect(boxes).toHaveLength(3)

  },
}
